title: Complexity of Differentially Private Selection via Federated APIs
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Aggregation-based and shuffle models incur high error for selection, while the proposed SVT primitive matches the central model's logarithmic error.
layout: 1 table, 2 rows by 4 columns, blue headers, ours-style contrast on last row
description: A compact comparison table with four blue bold column headers: SecAgg, Shuffle DP, SVT, and Central DP. Two bold row labels sit at left: Aggregation and Selection, separated from the header by a horizontal rule. Every cell holds a math fraction. The Aggregation row reads sqrt(d)/epsilon in all four columns. The Selection row reads sqrt(d)/epsilon under SecAgg and Shuffle DP, but log d / epsilon under SVT and Central DP. The eye goes first to the blue headers, then to the bottom-right cells where the error drops from sqrt(d) to log d. This shows that SVT closes the gap to the central model for selection, while SecAgg and shuffle remain stuck at the higher error.
caption: Comparison of the additive error achievable for the different APIs in the federated setting, up to constant factors, for n users. In the aggregation row each user holds a vector of ℓ2 norm at most 1 and the error is the ℓ2 error of the sum. In the selection row each user holds scores in [0, 1]d and the error is the additive error in the sum score; the entry d/ε). The entries for SVT and central DP are upper bounds (ε-DP, Theorem 2.2 for SVT with n polynomial in d). The entries for SecAgg and shuffle DP are lower bounds: for algorithms that access the data through an aggregation API (Theorem 4.4), and for robust or single-round shuffle protocols (Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.4).
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) has become the standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, yet its practical implementation in federated or distributed settings often faces a significant utility gap compared to the central model. While existing frameworks, including local, shuffle, and secure aggregation models, offer vetted primitives, they can incur high error for important tasks such as selection. Our first contribution is to show that this is inherent in the aggregation model: any private selection algorithm relying on the standard noisy aggregation primitive requires $Î©(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)$ samples. To address this limitation, we propose adding a new primitive that implements a version of the Sparse Vector Technique (SVT) and argue that it has simple implementations under various trust models. We demonstrate its power by developing an $\varepsilon$-differentially private algorithm for the selection problem. For selection in dimension $d$, our algorithm achieves an additive error of $O\left(\frac{\log(dn)}{\varepsilon}\right)$, matching that of the central model when $n$ is polynomially bounded in $d$. Furthermore, we show that this can be done using a near-optimal expected number $O(d\log^*d)$ of SVT queries. Together with existing lower bounds for the shuffle model, this result establishes an exponential separation between the SVT model and shuffle or aggregation-based models. We demonstrate the model's broad applicability to diverse tasks such as $F_p$ loss minimization, heavy-hitter identification, and sparse mean estimation.
